headline: Medium-risk pair: shared networked, browser-capable agents can exchange untrusted outputs and leak sensitive context, but no direct shared workspace is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can run browsers and use network egress, so one can ingest untrusted web content that the other may later consume. LightAgent also uses MCP and stdin/stdout, while RD-Agent has API-driven workflows and logs, creating plausible instruction-smuggling paths. No shared filesystem is documented, so this is not high.
conditions: IF LightAgent forwards browser text into MCP/tool prompts without sanitization, injection is possible.
IF RD-Agent consumes LightAgent-produced text as instructions rather than data, hijacking becomes feasible.
mitigations: Disable automatic prompt ingestion from browser output.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages.
Require a human review step before tool execution.
Strip executable-looking markup from copied content.
requires-engineering: enforce schema-validated message passing between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightAgent handles user conversations, long-term memory, tool results, and secrets, while RD-Agent touches financial reports, papers, datasets, logs, and API keys. Both have broad network egress, so sensitive material could leave the pair through model/API calls. No shared workspace is documented, so the leak path is indirect rather than guaranteed.
conditions: IF either agent sends its full context window to a third-party API, sensitive data can leak.
IF both agents are pointed at the same sensitive corpus, cross-exposure becomes possible.
mitigations: Remove secrets from prompts before handoff.
Use separate API keys per agent.
Limit logs to redacted metadata.
Review outbound destinations in both configs.
requires-engineering: isolate workspaces and enforce per-agent data boundaries.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances and broad network egress, so concurrent writes to shared mutable resources are plausible if the operator points them at the same APIs or files. LightAgent can spawn subprocesses and use MCP; RD-Agent uses APIs and logs. No locking or shared-dir isolation is documented, so conflict risk exists but is not proven high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same external resource without locking, state corruption can occur.
IF the operator shares one mutable workspace or API account, concurrent updates may collide.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Use distinct API accounts or projects.
Serialize writes with a simple manual lock file.
Check for existing artifacts before writing.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control to shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightAgent can emit tool results, provenance metadata, and workflow state; RD-Agent is a research automation system that can act on outputs via APIs and logs. If RD-Agent treats LightAgent output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The profiles do not show verification gates, so the pathway is plausible in default use but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF RD-Agent ingests LightAgent output without validation, incorrect facts can propagate.
IF LightAgent fabricates provenance metadata that RD-Agent trusts, downstream decisions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require source citations before actioning outputs.
Add a second-pass verifier for critical claims.
Keep LightAgent outputs advisory only.
Log and diff all handoffs between agents.
requires-engineering: implement confidence thresholds before RD-Agent acts.

E_compliance.rationale: LightAgent handles user conversations, long-term memory, and secrets; RD-Agent handles financial reports, competition datasets, and logs. If regulated or region-bound data is routed through both, retention and residency obligations may diverge. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so the mismatch is plausible but not specific to one jurisdiction.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in LightAgent memory and also logged by RD-Agent, retention mismatch arises.
IF EU or sector-regulated data is processed through both agents, residency or policy conflicts may occur.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent.
Disable logging of sensitive payloads.
Keep regulated datasets out of shared workflows.
Review retention settings for both systems.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across the pair.
